items.prompt: Why do the stars appear to wheel slowly around a single fixed point over the course of one night?

options.label: Earth is turning on its own axis, and that axis points toward one particular direction in the sky that barely seems to shift
options.feedback: As Earth spins, everything overhead appears to sweep around in the opposite direction; the one point in the sky that lines up with Earth's own spin axis is the single spot that doesn't join in that sweep, so everything else looks to circle around it.

options.label: Every star in the sky is genuinely orbiting one particular central star
options.feedback: The stars visible at night are scattered through space at wildly different distances and have no shared central star they all circle; the apparent wheeling comes from Earth's own spin, not from any real orbit among the stars themselves.

options.label: Wind currents in the upper atmosphere slowly carry the stars sideways
options.feedback: The stars sit far beyond Earth's atmosphere entirely, well out of reach of any wind or air current; nothing about atmospheric motion could carry them around the sky.

options.label: The stars actually stay still, and it is only an optical illusion with no real motion behind it
options.feedback: There is a real motion behind the apparent sweep, just not in the stars themselves — it is Earth's own steady spin that produces the effect, not an illusion arising from nothing at all.

items.ok_line: It's Earth doing the turning, not the stars.
items.ko_line: Nothing in the sky is orbiting anything else overnight — the motion is happening much closer to home.
items.exp_text: Earth completes a full turn on its own axis roughly once a day, and from the surface of something spinning, everything that isn't spinning along with it appears to sweep past in the opposite direction. The one direction in the sky that lines up with Earth's own axis of spin is the single point that doesn't take part in that apparent sweep, so every other star, unmoving in reality, appears from here to trace a slow circle around it.

items.prompt: Why does one particular point in the sky, near where the pole star sits, stay in almost the same spot all night while every other star sweeps around in a wide circle?

options.label: That point lies almost exactly along the direction Earth's own axis of rotation points, so Earth's spin barely shifts its apparent position at all
options.feedback: A star positioned nearly along the extension of Earth's own spin axis sits almost precisely at the center of the sky's apparent daily rotation, so as Earth turns, that star's own apparent position moves only very slightly, while every other direction sweeps through a wide circle around it.

options.label: That particular star has stopped moving through space entirely
options.feedback: The pole star is still moving through space just like any other star; what makes it look fixed has nothing to do with its own motion, but with how it happens to line up with Earth's spin axis as seen from here.

options.label: That star is much closer to Earth than the others, so it doesn't appear to move
options.feedback: How close or far a star is doesn't determine whether it appears to circle the sky each night; that apparent circling depends on its direction relative to Earth's spin axis, not on its distance.

options.label: Earth briefly stops spinning once each night, right around that direction
options.feedback: Earth's spin never pauses for any part of the sky; it turns at a steady rate throughout, and the apparent stillness near the pole comes from that direction lining up with the axis Earth spins around, not from any pause in the spin.

items.ok_line: Sitting almost exactly on the axis Earth spins around.
items.ko_title: Think about the axis, not the star
items.ko_line: This one star isn't special in itself — it just happens to sit in line with the direction Earth is spinning around.
items.exp_title: The eye of the turning sky
items.exp_text: As Earth spins, the entire sky appears to wheel around a central point that lines up with the direction of Earth's own axis, the way the middle of a spinning wheel barely moves while its rim sweeps past. A star positioned very close to that exact direction sits almost precisely at that unmoving center, so while every other star traces a wide circle over the course of the night, this one shifts hardly at all.

items.prompt: Why do some stars near the pole never dip below the horizon, while other stars rise and set every day like the sun does?

options.label: Stars close enough to the pole trace a circle around it that stays entirely above the horizon from a given place, while stars farther from the pole trace a wider circle that dips below it
options.feedback: How wide a circle a star traces around the sky's fixed point depends on how far the star sits from that point; a star close enough to the pole has a circle small enough to stay entirely above the horizon as seen from a given place, while a star farther from the pole sweeps through a wider circle that carries it below the horizon for part of each day.

options.label: The stars that never set are much brighter than the ones that do
options.feedback: How bright a star looks has no bearing on whether its daily circle around the sky carries it below the horizon; that depends only on how close the star sits to the sky's fixed pole, as seen from a given place.

options.label: Stars that never set are somehow not affected by Earth's spin at all
options.feedback: Every star, without exception, takes part in the same apparent daily sweep caused by Earth's spin; a star that never sets is still circling, it's simply circling on a path small enough to stay entirely above the horizon throughout.

options.label: The stars that set do so because they are much farther away in distance
options.feedback: Distance to a star doesn't decide whether it rises and sets; what decides that is only how close the star's position lies to the sky's fixed pole as seen from a given place on Earth.

items.ok_line: A tight circle near the pole stays above the horizon all the way round.
items.ko_title: Think about the size of the circle
items.ko_line: Every star is circling the same fixed point — ask how wide a circle each one traces, and whether that circle clears the horizon.
items.exp_title: Some circles clear the horizon, some don't
items.exp_text: Every star traces a circle around the sky's fixed pole once each day as Earth spins, and how wide that circle is depends entirely on how far the star sits from that pole. A star close to the pole traces a small enough circle to stay above the horizon the entire way around, while one farther out sweeps through a circle so wide that part of it inevitably dips below the horizon, carrying that star out of sight for part of each day.

items.prompt: Why do you see a different set of constellations filling the night sky in winter than in summer?

options.label: Earth's yearly orbit around the sun changes which stars lie opposite the sun, and so which stars appear in the night sky, as the months pass
options.feedback: At any given point along its orbit, Earth's night side faces a particular direction out into space; as Earth moves around the sun over the course of a year, that direction steadily shifts, sweeping the night side to face a different backdrop of stars in each season.

options.label: The stars themselves move to new positions between winter and summer
options.feedback: The pattern of stars stays essentially fixed relative to one another across a single year; what changes with the seasons is which direction Earth's night side happens to be facing, not the stars' own positions.

options.label: Some constellations only exist during certain months and vanish afterward
options.feedback: A constellation's stars continue to exist year-round; a constellation seems to disappear for part of the year only because Earth's orbit has carried its night side to face away from that patch of sky for a while, not because the stars themselves come and go.

options.label: Cloud cover consistently differs between the two seasons, hiding certain stars in one and not the other
options.feedback: This seasonal change in the visible constellations happens even on perfectly clear nights in both seasons; it comes from Earth's changing position along its orbit, not from any difference in cloud cover.

items.ok_line: Earth's orbit turns the night side to face a different patch of stars.
items.ko_title: Think about which way night faces
items.ko_line: The stars haven't gone anywhere — ask which direction Earth's night side is pointing at different times of year.
items.exp_text: At any moment, the side of Earth experiencing night is the side turned away from the sun, and that facing direction points out toward one particular patch of the surrounding sky and its stars. As Earth travels along its year-long orbit, the direction the sun sits in keeps changing, and so does the opposite direction the night side faces, which is why the backdrop of stars overhead after dark looks different in December than it does in June.

items.prompt: Why does what's visible in the night sky depend on which hemisphere of Earth an observer is standing in?

options.label: The direction of the sky's pole, and therefore which stars stay always visible or always hidden, depends on which way the observer's local ground is tilted relative to Earth's axis
options.feedback: Standing on Earth's surface, the ground beneath an observer's feet blocks half the full sky, and which half depends on the local tilt relative to Earth's axis; that means a different pole, and a different set of always-visible or never-visible stars, for observers in each hemisphere.

options.label: Stars actually appear brighter on one side of Earth than on the other
options.feedback: A star's brightness as seen from Earth doesn't depend on which hemisphere the observer stands in; what changes between hemispheres is which stars are visible at all, not how bright any given star looks.

options.label: Earth's atmosphere is noticeably thinner over one hemisphere than the other
options.feedback: Earth's atmosphere is broadly similar in thickness worldwide; the difference in visible sky between hemispheres comes from geometry, the tilt of the local ground relative to Earth's axis, not from any difference in the air above.

options.label: The two hemispheres are different distances from the stars being observed
options.feedback: The stars are so enormously far away compared with the width of Earth itself that the tiny difference in distance between one hemisphere and the other makes no meaningful difference to what can be seen; what matters instead is the direction each hemisphere faces.

items.ok_line: Different ground, different tilt, a different half of the sky blocked.
items.ko_title: Think about the tilt of the ground
items.ko_line: The stars are the same everywhere on Earth — what changes is which half of the sky the ground itself blocks from view.
items.exp_title: Half a sky, and a different half at that
items.exp_text: Standing anywhere on Earth's surface, the solid ground underfoot blocks exactly half of the full sphere of sky at any moment, and which half is blocked depends on how the local ground is tilted relative to the direction of Earth's spin axis. Because that tilt points in opposite senses for the northern and southern hemispheres, each side of Earth has its own pole overhead and its own set of stars that stay permanently visible or permanently hidden, different from the other hemisphere's.

items.prompt: Why do the stars making up a single constellation look grouped together in the sky, even though they can be nowhere near each other in actual space?

options.label: They only happen to lie along nearly the same line of sight from Earth, regardless of how far apart they truly are in three-dimensional space
options.feedback: Looking out from one single vantage point flattens every direction onto the dome of the sky, so two stars can appear side by side there simply because they line up along nearly the same direction from Earth, even if one sits vastly farther away than the other.

options.label: The stars in a constellation are always genuinely close neighbors in space
options.feedback: Stars that appear grouped together in a constellation are often separated by enormous, wildly differing distances in actual space; what groups them in the sky is simply that they happen to lie in almost the same direction as seen from Earth, not any real closeness.

options.label: Gravity pulls the stars of a constellation into a fixed pattern relative to one another
options.feedback: Stars within a constellation are typically far too distant from one another, and moving on far too independent paths, for gravity between them to hold any fixed pattern together; the grouping is only an apparent one, based on shared direction as seen from here.

options.label: All the stars in any one constellation formed together from the very same cloud of gas
options.feedback: Stars grouped into a constellation generally have entirely separate histories and origins; sharing a constellation is only a matter of appearing in roughly the same direction from Earth, not of any shared birthplace.

items.ok_line: Same direction from here, not the same neighborhood out there.
items.ko_line: Being lined up as seen from one point is very different from actually being close together.
items.exp_title: A pattern flattened onto one dome
items.exp_text: Viewed from any single point, every direction out into space collapses onto the flat-looking dome of the sky, so two stars can appear right next to each other there for no reason beyond happening to sit along nearly the same line of sight from that one point. Their true distances from Earth, and from each other, can differ enormously, meaning a constellation's stars are grouped only by shared direction as seen from here, not by any real closeness out in space.

items.prompt: Why does every star's light reach the eye as a single point, no matter how physically enormous the star actually is?

options.label: A star's true width takes up such a tiny angle in the sky, owing to its enormous distance, that the eye cannot perceive it as anything but a point
options.feedback: However large a star truly is across, its distance is so much larger still that the angle its width spans in the sky shrinks down to something far smaller than the eye is able to resolve, leaving only a point of light no matter the star's real size.

options.label: Every star is genuinely a similar, fairly small size, roughly comparable to one another
options.feedback: Stars differ enormously from one another in their true physical size; the reason every one still looks like a single point has nothing to do with them actually being similar in size, but with how small an angle even a huge star's width spans at such extreme distance.

options.label: Starlight travels in narrow, point-like beams rather than spreading outward
options.feedback: A star radiates its light outward in every direction from its whole surface, not as a narrow beam aimed anywhere in particular; the point-like appearance comes from the extreme distance shrinking the star's apparent width, not from the shape of the light it gives off.

options.label: The eye can only ever detect a single point of light at any one time from any one source
options.feedback: The eye is fully capable of resolving width and detail in a nearby, large-appearing object; it is the extreme distance to a star that shrinks its true width down below what the eye can resolve, not any general limitation on registering more than one point from a single source.

items.ok_line: Enormous, but so far away its width shrinks to nothing.
items.ko_title: Think about angle, not true size
items.ko_line: The star's true size isn't the issue — ask how small an angle even a huge width spans across such an extreme distance.
items.exp_title: Too far for its width to show
items.exp_text: How wide something appears in the sky depends on the true width divided by its distance, and for a star, however physically enormous, the distance involved is so much greater that the resulting angle shrinks down to an amount far too small for the eye to make out as anything with width at all. Lacking any perceptible width, the star's light reaches the eye indistinguishable from a source with no size whatsoever, which is why it looks like nothing more than a single point.

items.prompt: Why can a whole galaxy such as Andromeda be seen with the naked eye as a faint, fuzzy patch, while none of the billions of individual stars making it up can be picked out on their own?

options.label: The combined light of its many stars spreads over a patch of sky wide enough to register as a glow, even though each single star within it is far too faint on its own to be seen individually
options.feedback: Any one star inside such a distant galaxy is, by itself, far too dim to register to the naked eye, but the light of a huge number of them together, spread across the small patch of sky the galaxy occupies, adds up to a combined glow just bright enough to be noticed as one faint, fuzzy smudge.

options.label: Andromeda is actually a single enormous star rather than a whole galaxy
options.feedback: The fuzzy patch is the combined light of an enormous number of separate stars bound together as a galaxy, not the light of one single giant star.

options.label: The galaxy is close enough that its individual stars can, in fact, be picked out one by one with the naked eye
options.feedback: Even the nearest large galaxy beyond our own sits at a distance so great that no single star within it can be told apart from the rest with the naked eye; only their light blended together is bright enough to notice at all.

options.label: It glows because it reflects light from stars in our own galaxy
options.feedback: The glow of a distant galaxy comes from the light of its own countless stars shining under their own power, not from light reflected off anything belonging to our own galaxy.

items.ok_line: Individually too faint, but their combined light adds up to a glow.
items.ko_line: No single star there could ever be seen alone — ask what happens when the light of a huge number of them is added together.
items.exp_title: Too faint alone, bright enough together
items.exp_text: Any one star inside a galaxy as distant as Andromeda sends far too little light to Earth on its own to register to the naked eye at all. Spread across the small patch of sky the whole galaxy occupies, however, the combined light of its enormous number of stars adds up to just enough total brightness to be noticed as a single faint, fuzzy smudge, even though not one of the individual stars contributing to that glow can be picked out on its own.

items.prompt: Why is the daytime sky just as full of stars as the night sky, yet none of them can be seen while the sun is up?

options.label: Sunlight scattered by Earth's atmosphere fills the whole daytime sky with light far brighter than the faint light of any star, drowning the stars out
options.feedback: During the day, sunlight striking Earth's atmosphere gets scattered in every direction, filling the entire sky with a glow that vastly outshines the comparatively faint light reaching us from any star, so the stars are still there, simply overwhelmed rather than gone.

options.label: The stars themselves physically move to the other side of Earth during the day
options.feedback: Stars don't relocate over the course of a single day; the same stars remain in essentially the same positions relative to Earth whether it's day or night, they simply become impossible to pick out against the bright, sunlit sky.

options.label: Stars only produce light during the hours of night
options.feedback: A star shines continuously, at essentially the same steady brightness, regardless of whether it happens to be day or night on the side of Earth beneath it; what changes with daytime is not the star's output, but how much brighter the surrounding sky has become.

options.label: The sun's gravity temporarily pulls the stars out of view during the day
options.feedback: Gravity from the sun has no effect on how visible a star looks from Earth's surface; what hides the stars during the day is the bright, scattered sunlight filling the sky, not any pull on the stars' positions.

items.ok_line: Still there, just outshone by the scattered light of day.
items.ko_title: Think about what's overwhelming the light
items.ko_line: The stars haven't gone anywhere or stopped shining — ask what's filling the sky around them instead.
items.exp_text: Every star visible at night keeps shining with essentially the same steady output throughout the day as well, since a star's own light production has nothing to do with whatever is happening on Earth. What changes during the day is that sunlight striking the atmosphere gets scattered across the entire sky, filling it with a glow far brighter than any star's comparatively faint light, so the stars remain exactly where they always are, simply drowned out until that scattered daylight fades after sunset.

items.prompt: Why do the stars keep the same pattern relative to one another from night to night, even as the whole sky appears to sweep around over the course of each night?

options.label: The stars are so far away that their true motion through space barely shifts their relative positions on any timescale a person could notice, so only Earth's own fast spin makes the pattern appear to move as one rigid whole
options.feedback: Individual stars really are moving through space, but at such enormous distances that even fast true motion produces only an imperceptibly tiny shift in relative position over a human lifetime, while Earth's own spin, completing a full turn roughly once a day, is by comparison fast enough to carry the whole unchanging pattern sweeping across the sky together.

options.label: The stars are physically connected to one another by an invisible rigid frame
options.feedback: Nothing physically links one star to another; each moves independently through space under its own gravity and motion. What keeps the pattern looking rigid over a single night is simply that individual stellar motion is too slow to notice on that timescale, not any real connection between them.

options.label: Every star in the sky is completely motionless and has never moved at all
options.feedback: Every star is, in fact, moving through space; it only looks unmoving relative to its neighbors because that true motion is far too slow to notice against the vastly faster apparent sweep caused by Earth's own daily spin.

options.label: The pattern changes constantly, but far too quickly for the human eye to detect any of it
options.feedback: The pattern of stars relative to each other does shift, but far too slowly, not too quickly, for the eye to catch over the course of any single night; over many years, the slow, accumulating shift can eventually become detectable.

items.ok_line: Too far and too slow to notice — only Earth's spin is fast enough to see.
items.ko_title: Think about two very different speeds
items.ko_line: One kind of motion here is far too slow to notice, and another is fast enough to sweep the whole sky in a night — work out which is which.
items.exp_title: Two motions, two very different speeds
items.exp_text: Stars really do move through space, but from as far away as they are, that true motion shifts their positions relative to one another by amounts too small to notice over the course of any single night or even many nights in a row. Earth's own spin, by contrast, completes a full turn in about a day, fast enough for that motion alone to sweep the whole unchanging pattern of stars across the sky together, as one rigid dome turning overhead.
